ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Renal impairment and antacid accumulation

A 73-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease takes large doses of a magnesium-containing antacid for several days. He develops lethargy, hypotension and diminished deep-tendon reflexes. His serum magnesium is markedly elevated. Which pharmacokinetic change most directly explains his susceptibility?

  1. Reduced pulmonary excretion of magnesium
  2. Reduced renal elimination of absorbed magnesium
  3. Accelerated hepatic conversion of magnesium to an active metabolite
  4. Increased biliary recycling of unabsorbed magnesium
  5. Irreversible binding of magnesium to plasma albumin
Answer and explanation

Reduced renal elimination of absorbed magnesium

Impaired renal magnesium elimination allows even partially absorbed magnesium to accumulate.

Option explanations

Reduced renal elimination of absorbed magnesium: Kidney dysfunction limits clearance of absorbed magnesium.

Accelerated hepatic conversion of magnesium to an active metabolite: Magnesium is an element and is not converted into an active hepatic metabolite.

Increased biliary recycling of unabsorbed magnesium: Unabsorbed magnesium remains in the bowel; biliary recycling does not explain this toxicity.

Irreversible binding of magnesium to plasma albumin: Irreversible albumin binding is not the cause of magnesium accumulation.

Reduced pulmonary excretion of magnesium: The lungs are not the principal route of magnesium elimination.
